stem: A tree is a special graph with:
options: NO CYCLES and exactly one route between any two nodes
explanation: Graphs have no shape rules - cycles allowed, any connections. That freedom is why searches need a 'seen' set that trees never did.

stem: The adjacency LIST (node -> neighbours dictionary) beats a matrix when:
options: The graph is SPARSE - matrix memory is O(V squared) regardless of edges
explanation: Most real graphs are sparse. The matrix earns its place only when almost everything connects to almost everything.

stem: AddEdge for an undirected graph must:
options: Record the edge BOTH ways - forget the reverse and half the map is unreachable
explanation: adjacency[from].Add(to) AND adjacency[to].Add(from). A classic one-line omission with confusing symptoms.

stem: BFS is built from a QUEUE plus a HashSet where items are marked seen:
options: When ENQUEUED - via HashSet.Add's bool - or nodes queue twice
explanation: Mark-on-enqueue is the correctness detail: 3.2's if (seen.Add(x)) doing structural work. The 5.6 queue + 3.2 set, assembled.

stem: BFS finds the shortest UNWEIGHTED path because it explores:
options: In RINGS - everything one hop away before anything two hops away
explanation: You cannot reach ring 3 before exhausting ring 2, so the first arrival is via a minimal-hop route.

options: A STACK - or equivalently the call stack via recursion (5.4)
explanation: Charge down one path, backtrack, try the next. Less frontier memory; does NOT find shortest paths. Its homes: mazes, cycle detection, topological sort.

stem: ShortestPath rebuilds the route using a cameFrom dictionary by:
options: Walking BREADCRUMBS backwards from the end, then reversing
explanation: Record how each node was first reached; the trail end-to-start plus one Reverse() is the answer - A to F: A,B,D,E,F.

stem: Omitting the 'seen' set from graph search causes:
options: An INFINITE LOOP on the first cycle - A to B to A forever
explanation: The hazard trees never had. Cycles are legal in graphs; the seen set is what tames them.

stem: Dijkstra can prefer a FIVE-hop route over a four-hop one when:
options: The five hops COST LESS - it minimises total weight, not hop count (13 vs 14 in the lesson)
explanation: Fewest hops (BFS) and cheapest (Dijkstra) are different questions - your satnav taking three extra junctions to dodge the toll road.

stem: Dijkstra upgrades BFS by replacing the plain queue with:
options: A PRIORITY QUEUE always yielding the cheapest-known unexplored node (3.3)
explanation: Plus edge 'relaxation': if distance[node] + weight beats distance[to], record the cheaper way in. One caveat: no negative weights.
